When diesel is scarce and margins are strong, every planned maintenance day appears to sacrifice valuable output.

Product-tanker effects move in the opposite direction

When a refinery stops, its diesel, gasoline, jet, or naphtha exports decline.

A refinery cannot produce only diesel. Higher crude runs also make gasoline, fuel oil, LPG, naphtha, and other products, whose margins may be weaker. Tight jet demand can encourage kerosene yield at the expense of gasoil.

Oil tanker freight rates plunge in Asia as Strait of Hormuz attacks disrupt fuel shipments

OilNOW · November 19, 2026
Oil tanker freight rates across Asia-Pacific have fallen sharply as attacks on commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz disrupt refined fuel shipments, leaving more tankers competing for fewer cargoes.
S&P Global reported on November 18 that Medium Range (MR) tanker freight rates dropped by 125 Worldscale points on a benchmark Middle East route, as security concerns slowed vessel movements through the critical shipping passage.
“Cargo flows are limited; there are hardly any refined products coming out from the Persian Gulf. Several tankers are looking for employment and ready to snap up cargoes at lower rates,” a senior executive at a clean oil tanker company told S&P Global.
According to UK Maritime Trade Operations, three commercial vessels were attacked in the Persian Gulf and waters off Oman over two days.
Wood Mackenzie cuts Q4 global crude run forecast by 1.4 million b/d as Middle East conflict drags on
The growing risks have prompted many shipping companies to avoid the Strait, while others wait for vessels inside the Persian Gulf to transport fuel to ship-to-ship transfer locations in Oman and western India.
Daily vessel transits through Hormuz fell to just 14 on November 9, compared with 32 at the end of October, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea data. Brokers estimated that fewer than six refined-product tankers were passing through the Strait on an average day.
The disruption is already affecting freight negotiations.
Brokers reported that Vitol provisionally booked the Torm Stellar at Worldscale 500 for November 25 diesel loading on the Duqm-East Africa route. Another tanker, Weco Amalie, was subsequently placed at Worldscale 475 for the Sikka-East Africa route, representing a decline of 125 points from the previous comparable fixture.
Iran says U.S. failing to meet conditions for reopening of Hormuz Strait
The weakness has spread to North Asia, where refined-product exports from China have fallen short of expectations despite the government announcing approximately 5.65 million metric tons of additional export quotas in late October.
On the South Korea-Japan route, the Oriental Sunstone was provisionally booked for US$975,000, marking the first reported fixture below US$1 million since late August.
Lower MR freight rates are also prompting some charterers to consider splitting larger fuel shipments into smaller parcels rather than using Long Range (LR) tankers.

Tankers with Russian Diesel Reach Brazil After Bypassing the U.S.

oil protest with tanker Greenpeace was highlighting the track of the tankers (photo courtesy of Greepeace)
By The Maritime Executive 2026-11-19 15:58:16
Two tankers laden with Russian diesel arrived in Brazil as analysts continue to point out that none of the promised Russian product has reached the U.S. Speculation had centered on these and other tankers that departed Russia in mid-October as part of the agreement reached between Washington and Moscow for the supply of diesel.
Six weeks ago, the Trump administration had announced a deal promising that Russian diesel would be coming to the United States and returning to the international market to compensate for the shortages from the Persian Gulf. Russia had said it was ramping up production and shipments after temporarily suspending international shipments of diesel and gasoline in response to the continuing strikes by Ukraine on Russian refineries and oil terminals.
Russian officials highlighted the first shipment to the U.S. while speculation grew over the amount of diesel being exported. Trump administration officials promised up to 300,000 metric tons. Multiple tankers were identified, with the watchdog group Greenpeace tracking as many as 11 vessels at one point. Several turned out not to be loaded with diesel, while others fell off the tracking one by one as it became clear they were not sailing to the United States.
The Sierra Leone-flagged tanker Leruo (IMO 9385831) appears to be the first to reach its destination, the Itacoatiara anchorage in Brazil, where it arrived earlier this week. The 46,000-dwt product tanker had loaded at Primorsk. Its AIS  signal shows it is back underway, traveling along the Amazon to Manus. Close behind is the Russian-flagged product tanker Primorye (IMO 9236743), which has also reached the same anchorage. A third product tanker, the Sierra Leone-flagged Beast (IMO 9290921), is also sailing along the South American coast with its AIS signal reporting “Brazil For Orders.”
The Leruo is believed to have approximately 40,000 metric tons of diesel aboard. The other two product tankers have similar loads of diesel.
Speculation had been that all three of these tankers might have been bound for the U.S. before opposition grew over the shipments. While the administration issued a waiver, members of the U.S. Congress continued to voice opposition and cited the potential for legal issues, as all the tankers are operating under international sanctions. Governor Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey also published a letter warning terminal operators and fuel companies not to receive the cargo due to the potential for legal challenges. Even without the potential legal issues, anyone dealing in the Russian diesel faced bad publicity and harm to their reputation.
Ukraine highlighted the track record of the Leruo . It asserts the tanker has frequently turned off its AIS transmissions and conducted ship-to-ship transfers. They tracked the vessel making deliveries to Tripoli, Lebanon, in the past. The European Union sanctioned the product tanker in July 2025, followed by the UK in October and other countries.
Brazil, however, has been happy to receive the cargo. The Brazilian newspaper Gazeta do Povo cites data showing that Brazil has maintained a multibillion-dollar trade with Russia. It reports the value of Russian energy imports into Brazil at R$5 billion (US$840 million) so far in 2026. Citing data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, it reports Brazil has received 28 vessels from the Russian shadow fleet this year, with a total of 34 deliveries of Russian diesel. They estimate the imports have totalled 1.11 million metric tons as part of a total import volume of 4.3 million metric tons coming from Russia this year.
Other tankers that reports had speculated were bound for the United States have instead gone to destinations in the Mediterranean. The Russian-flagged product tanker Talisman (IMO 9292060), which, for example, had been another one identified in the reports as bound for the United States, has instead been spotted off Egypt.

...

It continues to sail back and forth several hundred miles out in the Atlantic with its AIS transmission as “For Orders.” The 50,000-dwt product tanker had been identified as the first to sail with Russian diesel bound for the United States, but continues to hold short of its destination.
It is unclear what will happen to the agreement the Trump administration had promoted just weeks ago. Reuters is reporting that since late October, Ukraine has “slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent.” The attacks Reuters reports have now disrupted or halted operations at 15 of Russia's 35 major refineries.

About the Strait of Hormuz

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the open ocean. Approximately 21% of global petroleum consumption passes through this chokepoint daily, making it the world's most important oil transit route. The strait is about 21 nautical miles (39 km) wide at its narrowest point, with shipping lanes about 2 nautical miles (3.7 km) wide in each direction. Read more in the FAQ .

How This Ship Tracker Works

This dashboard tracks vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz using AIS (Automatic Identification System) transponder data polled every 30 minutes. Ships are classified into two geographic zones — the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman — and crossings are detected when a vessel transitions between zones. The monitor tracks around 4,000 ships per poll cycle including tankers, bulk carriers, container ships, and LNG/LPG carriers. See About & Methodology for more details.

Public API

Ship traffic data is available via free JSON API endpoints. Access current ship positions at /api/ships , daily crossing statistics at /api/crossings/daily , and the full ship directory at /api/ships/directory . See the API documentation for every endpoint. In September alone Iraq shipped more crude to Turkey than Russia did. Total crude imports did not fall: they were 3.9% higher than in the first nine months of 2025. Iraq, Ceyhan and the Kirkuk line

Iraqi crude reaches Turkey two ways: by tanker from Basra, and by pipeline from the north to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
The pipeline route has spent much of the past three years shut. Exports through the Iraq-Turkey pipeline stopped in March 2023, after an International Chamber of Commerce ruling ordered Turkey to pay Iraq $1.5 billion in damages over oil exported without Baghdad's approval by the Kurdistan Regional Government. Kurdish crude began flowing again on September 27, 2025, at about 180,000 to 190,000 b/d, under a deal that lets Iraq's state marketer SOMO sell it (Reuters, September 27, 2025).
In 2026 the pipeline mattered more to Iraq than it had in years. The war with Iran that began in February 2026 disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz , and The National reported that Iraq's exports fell from 3.36 million b/d in February to 131,000 b/d in April. In August 2026 Turkey's BOTAS and Iraq's SOMO and North Oil Company signed a one-year interim extension of the pipeline agreement, which had expired in late July, at 750,000 b/d of transit capacity against a nameplate of 1.5 million b/d (Enerdata, August 4, 2026). On November 17, 2026 Iraq's oil minister said federal crude exports had resumed through the 960 km Kirkuk-Ceyhan line at an initial 120,000 b/d, with a goal of 500,000 b/d after repairs and tests.
Most crude loaded at Ceyhan is sold abroad, not refined in Turkey. Still, the route shows up in EPDK's figures: Iraq sold Turkey 4.75 million tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, almost as much as in all of 2025, during the same months that Hormuz traffic was disrupted. More on Iraq's export system is in our Iraq profile .

Is the Iraq-Turkey pipeline working?

Yes, as of November 2026. Kurdish crude has flowed to Ceyhan since September 27, 2025, and Iraq's oil minister said federal Kirkuk crude resumed on November 17, 2026 at 120,000 b/d, with a 500,000 b/d target. The transit deal was extended for one year in August 2026.

Baghdad Signals Tighter Grip Over KRG-Controlled Oilfields

Severity: WARNING Detected: 2026-11-24T06:18:09.310Z

Summary

Iraq’s oil minister accused the Kurdistan Regional Government of taking over federal oilfields and referenced investigations into northern oil smuggling, implying Baghdad intends to assert greater control over KRG-controlled assets. This raises near-term legal/export risk for KRG-linked crude flows through Turkey and could widen discounts on KBT/other Kurdish blends versus Brent.

Details

Iraq’s oil minister has publicly stated that the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has taken control of oilfields belonging to the federal North Oil Company and highlighted a completed investigation into oil smuggling in northern Iraq. While there is no explicit operational move yet (no announced field shutdown, pipeline closure, or arrests of operators), the rhetoric strongly suggests Baghdad is preparing to convert political-legal pressure into concrete measures to reassert control over KRG oil assets.
The immediate physical supply impact is zero, as exports from KRG fields via the Iraq–Turkey pipeline (to Ceyhan) have already been structurally constrained in recent years by legal disputes and Turkish pipeline downtime. However, markets will interpret this as an increased probability of: (1) new legal actions against international oil companies (IOCs) operating under KRG PSCs; (2) federal attempts to redirect offtake or payments; and (3) renewed friction over pipeline restart terms with Turkey. In a high-case escalation, up to ~350–400 kb/d of potential northern Iraqi exports (KRG + some federal volumes) could be kept off the seaborne market for longer than previously expected.
The key traded instruments affected are Brent and Dubai benchmarks, KBT and other Kurdish blend differentials, as well as equities/bonds of IOCs with KRG exposure. Directionally, this adds modest bullish pressure to medium-sour crude prices and widens perceived geopolitical/regulatory risk premia on Iraqi barrels. Compared with past episodes – e.g., the March 2023 Iraq–Turkey pipeline halt after the Paris arbitration ruling – today’s development is more a signaling event than an outright shock, but it pushes markets to fade expectations of a swift normalization of northern Iraqi flows.
Market reaction is likely to be in the low-single-digit percentage range in affected differentials rather than flat price, unless followed by concrete enforcement steps (field seizures, contract cancellations, or pipeline negotiations breaking down). The impact is therefore medium in intensity but potentially longer in duration: it reinforces a structural theme of fragmented Iraqi governance and recurring disruptions to northern export capacity for at least the next 6–18 months.
AFFECTED ASSETS: Brent Crude, Dubai Crude, Iraqi Kirkuk crude differentials, Kurdish KBT blend differentials, Equities of DNO, Genel Energy and KRG-exposed E&Ps

Iraqi oil minister says Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline could reach capacity of 500,000 bpd with repairs and upgrades
An Iraqi government forces member walks next to a pipeline at the Bai Hassan Oil Field, west of the northern Iraqi city of Kirkuk, on 19 October 2017 (Ahmad al-Rubaye/AFP)
MEE staff
Published date: 17 November 2026 20:58 GMT | Last update: 4 days 3 hours ago
Iraq has resumed the pumping of crude oil for export through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan Pipeline to Turkey , as it looks to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
Iraq plans to pump up to 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil through the 960km-long pipeline that runs from the Iraqi city to Turkey’s Mediterranean port, Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Khudair said in a statement reported by the state-owned Iraqi News Agency on Tuesday.
He said the flow could reach 500,000 bpd after “successful completion of maintenance, rehabilitation, technical and operational tests” on the pipeline, which has been shuttered for more than a decade.
Iraq is one of the countries hardest hit by the US and Iran’s competing blockades in the Strait of Hormuz. Nearly all of Iraq’s oil exports exited the waterway before the US-Israeli war on Iran, and revenue from sales contributed to 90 percent of Iraq’s budget.
Restarting oil flows from Kirkuk to Ceyhan is the first step in Iraq’s efforts to reduce its dependence on Hormuz. Baghdad wants to connect Basra, its energy hub in southern Iraq, to the Mediterranean via the Syrian port of Baniyas and Turkey’s port of Ceyhan.

ERBIL (Kurdistan24) - A source at Iraq’s State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) said that 102,000 barrels per day of Kurdistan Region oil and 69,000 barrels per day of Kirkuk oil have been sold through the Kurdistan Region pipeline to Türkiye’s Ceyhan port, along with 168,000 barrels by land.
The source told Kurdistan24 on Thursday that from Nov. 1 to 18, Iraq as a whole sold more than 63 million barrels of oil. That brought its daily sales average to 3.5 million barrels.
According to the source’s breakdown, the Region’s oil sold at 102,000 barrels per day. Kirkuk oil, moved through the Kurdistan Region pipeline to Ceyhan, sold at 69,000 barrels per day, while Iraq also sold 168,000 barrels per day by the land route.
Those figures come as Iraq’s draft 2027 budget sets export estimates of its own. It puts the country’s total exports at 3.3 million barrels at a price of $60, while Article 10 binds the Region to export 445,000 barrels.
The source added that Iraq’s overall production has passed five million barrels, under OPEC’s export limit of 4.33 million barrels.
The current exports follow a long interruption. Exports of oil from the Kurdistan Region and Kirkuk stopped on March 25, 2023, after the Paris arbitration decision, and the halt lasted more than two years and six months. They resumed on Sept. 27, 2025, under a tripartite agreement between Baghdad, Erbil, and the oil companies.

US aims to grow mineral stockpile

* Market: Metals
* 11/11/26
The US Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) awarded up to $3.3bn in firm, fixed-price indefinite quantity/indefinite delivery (IDIQ) contracts for cobalt, gallium, nickel and high purity aluminum for the national defense stockpile, prompting questions over the quantities to actually be purchased.
Under an IDIQ contract, the agency may place purchases during the established ordering period under a maximum total purchasing amount, although the agency is not obligated to buy that volume or value. The awarded values represent ceilings of what could be spent under the IDIQ contracts and are not guaranteed purchases.
None of the acquisitions were announced officially by the awardee companies, but a spokesperson for the DLA noted awardees can choose to publicly share deals. Since the beginning of 2025 Metallus , Elmet , Largo , US Antimony and Global Advanced Metals all shared public updates on awards with the agency for strategic materials.
The DLA committed $2bn to acquiring strategic and critical materials for the national defense stockpile throughout fiscal year 2026 (1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026), including high purity aluminum, according to an agency press release.
Previously, the DLA would release the Annual Materials Plan (AMP), a list of potential material acquisitions including maximum quantities to be purchased, at the beginning of the agency's fiscal year in October. The DLA never released an AMP for the 2026 fiscal year and has yet to release one for 2027, leaving market participants still mulling which materials the agency already secured and what will be prioritized.

Cobalt

Switzerland-based miner and trader Glencore secured a contract to supply cobalt worth up to $900mn over a five-year period, according to an updated filing on the agency's procurement website.
The DLA declined to comment on the quantity of material to be purchased. Glencore declined to comment on the award.

The agency initially requested quotes for up to 16.5mn lb (7,480t) of alloy-grade cobalt cut cathode or rounds in August 2025 for a maximum of $500mn before the tender was cancelled . Ultimately, the request was not competed.

Nickel

Glencore was also awarded a separate contract from the DLA for up to $65mn to supply 1,500t of nickel cathodes and pellets over a five-year ordering period beginning in September.
The agency initially issued a request for information on class 1 nickel products in March 2026 for 3,500t.
Argus obtained a copy of the nickel contract from the DLA internet bid board system, where it was posted publicly for a time alongside other non-ferrous contracts for the national defense stockpile, including the gallium contract, before being pulled.
After viewing the nickel contract, market participants surveyed by Argus posed few questions with some noting the expected volume to be purchased was relatively small and likely would not impact the market.

Aluminum

The Department of Defense announced Rio Tinto was awarded up to $995mn to supply high purity aluminum to the DLA on 25 September, noting it was a competitive acquisition with three responses received.
The company will supply "a small volume" of high purity aluminum, Rio Tinto confirmed, but did not provide further details as to how much material the company could supply over the five-year period.
Aluminum roller Arconic also received an IDIQ award to supply high purity aluminum for up to $995mn over a five-year period. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
The Department of Defense awarded Arconic $45.5mn in 2023 to boost production of high purity aluminum for missiles and munitions.

Gallium

The DLA awarded Louisiana-based alumina producer Atlantic Alumina (Atalco) a contract to supply up to $350mn for 55,610kg (55.6t) of gallium over a five-year ordering period.
Atalco did not immediately provide comment to Argus . The DOD has invested $400mn in the company, with a portion of the equity financing going toward scaling primary gallium production. The company expects to make 50t/yr of the semiconductor input once begins producing commercial volumes.

US reports $2B in mineral stockpile commitments

Tungsten is a vital defence component like in this F-16 over Las Vegas in 2012. ( Source: USAF Master Sgt. Benjamin Bloker via Wikimedia Commons ).
By: Staff Writer November 9, 2026
The U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) says it committed $2 billion (C$2.8 billion) to acquire strategic and critical materials for the National Defense Stockpile during fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 30.
The agency disclosed the total in a Nov. 5 announcement but did not identify the contracts, suppliers or quantities involved, or say how much had been paid out or delivered.
“These efforts are helping domestic companies plan production, retain skilled workers and expand capacity where economically viable,” DLA Strategic Materials director Eric Mata said in the release.
The fiscal-year tally updates Washington’s efforts to turn government buying power into reliable mineral supplies. DLA’s lithium tender delays in July highlighted the difficulty of converting purchasing plans into physical material, even as the government seeks to reduce dependence on foreign sources.

Existing commitments

The Pentagon’s stockpiling campaign was already under way in October 2025, when it moved to acquire up to $1 billion of critical minerals, the Financial Times reported.
Congress provided $2 billion for the stockpile through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed in July 2025, with the money available through fiscal 2029. In its April budget submission , DLA said authority to use that appropriation came in fiscal 2026.
DLA did not explain how the latest total relates to that funding or to previously announced contracts.
For example, The Elmet Group (Nasdaq: ELMT) announced a tungsten supply contract in September with a ceiling of $2 billion and a guaranteed minimum commitment of $150 million. The company said deliveries would wait until additional supply became available. That contract ceiling cannot be treated as another $2 billion of committed spending.
The defence stockpile is also separate from Project Vault , the reserve for manufacturers backed by Export-Import Bank of the United States financing. Project Vault was preparing to offer up to $1 billion in loans to manufacturers in October.

Domestic supply

The National Defense Stockpile holds materials for military and essential civilian needs during national emergencies, when commercial supplies may fall short. Most of DLA’s critical mineral contracts were intended to encourage domestic production, Mata said.
Materials sourced for the stockpile can range from high-purity aluminum to vanadium pentoxide, DLA said, without identifying the materials covered by the latest total. Recovery and recycling can provide additional domestic sources where technically and economically feasible, Mata said.
“Domestic sourcing is especially important when a material is essential to national defense, is subject to concentrated or vulnerable supply chains, is difficult to replace, and is not readily available from reliable sources in the quantities or forms required,” Mata said. “In those cases, domestic acquisition and stockpiling can help reduce single-point-of-failure risks, sustain U.S. industrial capability, and preserve material availability during disruption.”

The US needs more aluminium, but new smelters are years away

Edited by : Staff Editor
6 min read
The US needs more aluminium, but new smelters are years away
Stock image for referential purposes only
The US urgently needs more aluminium for its defence sector, but new smelters will take years to come online, while disruptions to high-purity aluminium imports have exposed a more immediate supply vulnerability.
The United States is facing a growing aluminium supply challenge that is becoming increasingly important for its defence sector, as rebuilding domestic production capacity remains a long-term process and overseas supply disruptions threaten access to specialised metal.
President Donald Trump recently said the US “desperately” needs more aluminium, highlighting the urgency facing a market that remains heavily dependent on imports despite efforts to revive domestic production.
One of the most prominent new projects is the planned aluminium smelter in Inola, Oklahoma, a joint venture between US producer Century Aluminum and Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA). The project has received USD 500 million in federal funding and is intended to strengthen US aluminium production.
But the project illustrates the problem facing the US: even if construction begins as scheduled by the end of 2026, the smelter is not expected to produce its first hot metal for at least another three years.
Pentagon faces an aluminium problem now
The urgency became clear during a US Department of Defense wargame conducted in July 2025 to examine the country's aluminium resilience in the event of a large-scale conflict in 2027.
The exercise brought together 80 participants from across the aluminium supply chain, industry associations and government departments to examine potential disruptions and policy responses.
The options included building new smelters, refurbishing existing facilities and increasing aluminium recycling. While these measures could improve the overall health of the US aluminium industry, the Defense Logistics Agency warned that none would meet the Department of Defense's shorter-term aluminium and high-purity aluminium requirements within two years.
The US can invest in new production capacity, but new facilities require years to build. Defence planners, meanwhile, need to know where their aluminium will come from if supply is disrupted during a major conflict.

High-purity aluminium exposes a bigger vulnerability
The most immediate concern is not necessarily ordinary aluminium, but high-purity aluminium (HPA).
The US defence sector accounts for only around 5 per cent of domestic aluminium demand, but its share is significantly higher when it comes to HPA. The specialised material, often used in alloy form, is required for some of the Pentagon's essential systems.
The US has only one domestic HPA producer, leaving the defence sector heavily reliant on imports.
A significant portion of those imports has historically come from the United Arab Emirates, making the supply chain particularly vulnerable to disruption in the Gulf.
That vulnerability became more apparent after Iran attacked EGA's Al Taweelah smelter in March. EGA has begun restoring operations, with a quarter of its electrolytic cells operational as of Wednesday, but US imports from the UAE have fallen sharply since the attack.
The Pentagon had already conducted another wargame examining potential disruptions at domestic facilities, including Alcoa's smelter in New York and Arconic's HPA plant in Iowa.
However, that exercise did not anticipate an attack on the US military's largest overseas HPA supplier.
The disruption has also complicated one of the simplest short-term solutions identified by the defence wargame: building up HPA and HPA-alloy stockpiles.
Tariffs have not closed the supply gap
Washington's 50 per cent aluminium import tariff has encouraged some domestic production to return, but the impact on overall supply has so far been limited.
Century Aluminum has restarted 50,000 tonnes per year of capacity at its Mount Holly smelter in South Carolina, bringing the facility back to full production.
Meanwhile, Magnitude 7 Metals is working to restart a 1970s-era smelter in Missouri that was closed in 2024. Its first 75,000-tonne-per-year potline is targeted for restart by the end of 2026.
Recycling is also expanding. According to the Aluminum Association, employment growth in the US aluminium recycling sector exceeded 20 per cent between 2024 and 2026.
But these developments have not eliminated the country's dependence on overseas metal.
The US remained 60 per cent dependent on aluminium imports in 2025, according to the US Geological Survey.

...

Canada could provide a short-term answer
The Trump administration has introduced another incentive: a reduced 25 per cent import tariff for companies building, expanding or refurbishing domestic aluminium smelting capacity. Canada, however, is not expected to receive the same reduction after trade negotiations broke down and tariffs escalated.
That is significant because Canada remains the largest supplier of primary aluminium to the US market, although it has directed more of its production towards Europe in recent months.
Even if Canada redirected its entire production towards the US, however, it would not be enough to eliminate the country's aluminium shortfall, according to Morgan Stanley analysts. The marginal imported tonne would still face a 50 per cent tariff, with the Midwest Premium reflecting the additional cost.
Yet Canada could still offer something the US urgently needs: a short-term supply buffer for defence.

...

And when it comes to high-purity aluminium, recent disruption in the UAE has shown just how exposed that gap can become.

Middle East conflict revives Pentagon concerns over US high-purity aluminium supply

Edited by : Nilanjana Banerjee
4 min read
Middle East conflict revives Pentagon concerns over US high-purity aluminium supply
Stock image for referential purposes only
A Pentagon-led simulation has brought fresh attention to the US’ dependence on imported high-purity aluminium, a critical raw material used in military aircraft, armoured vehicles and other defence applications. Conducted months before recent disruptions spurred by the Middle East conflict, the exercise had the US aluminium supply chain in focus.
It examined how the US aluminium supply chain would respond during a major geopolitical conflict and identified high-purity aluminium as one of the most exposed segments of the country’s defence industrial base. The findings have gained renewed relevance following the Iranian missile attacks on the aluminium facilities of Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA) and Aluminium Bahrain (Alba) in the Middle East or Gulf region on March 28, 2026.
Although repairs are running a head of schedule and production has since resumed at some plants, supply routes and output recovery remain under close watch , highlighting the importance of resilient aluminium supply chains for strategic industries.

Heavy reliance on imported high-purity aluminium
According to the exercise report, the simulation concluded that the US remains heavily reliant on overseas suppliers for high-purity aluminium. While China dominates global primary aluminium production, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has emerged as the principal supplier of the ultra-refined grade imported into the US, accounting for an estimated 90 per cent of imports used for defence-related applications.
High-purity aluminium contains exceptionally low levels of iron and silicon, making it suitable for manufacturing specialised alloys used in fighter aircraft and other defence equipment.
The exercise also highlighted a structural challenge for the US market. Domestic large-scale production of high-purity aluminium effectively ended in 2022 after the country’s last major producer ceased operations due to rising energy costs. As defence demand increases globally, restoring domestic capacity by stockpiling high-purity aluminium and associated products has become a growing topic of discussion among policymakers and industry participants.
Bill Greenwalt, Senior Fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and former Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Industrial Policy, described the situation as “a huge wake-up call for the department to be looking at supply chains in all areas around the world to ensure that they’re not especially vulnerable to attack or sabotage.”
Industry sources say that the market is not facing an outright shortage, but primary aluminium supplies remain tight . Much of the material used by US defence manufacturers seems to be sourced from EGA, before being processed by companies such as Kaiser Aluminum, Constellium and Arconic.
Commenting on the market, Uday Patel, Senior Research Manager for global aluminium markets at Wood Mackenzie, said, “We’re in a situation where there is no solution. Much will depend on how much stocks are in the pipeline.”

Policy recommendations focus on rebuilding domestic capacity
The war game, held over two days in July 2025 and overseen by the Institute for Defense Analyses, asked participants to assess how the US aluminium industry could respond if imports were disrupted during a large-scale conflict while domestic production also faced unexpected outages.
Participants recommended building strategic reserves of high-purity aluminium, expanding domestic production, investing in additional processing capacity and improving access to reliable, affordable power, an essential requirement for aluminium production.
The exercise forms part of wider efforts by the US government to identify vulnerabilities in critical mineral and manufacturing supply chains. Alongside supply diversification, policymakers are also examining ways to strengthen visibility across lower-tier suppliers that support the defence sector.
Charles Johnson, President and CEO of the Aluminum Association, said the findings reinforce the close relationship between industrial capability and national security, stating that “America’s military readiness is inseparable from America’s industrial readiness.” The association continues to advocate measures aimed at strengthening domestic aluminium production and processing.
Recent US policy initiatives like higher aluminium tariffs and incentives for new smelting capacity echo those objectives. However, industry observers note that establishing new high-purity aluminium production will require substantial investment, long development timelines and access to competitive energy supplies.
As geopolitical risks continue to influence global metals markets, the Pentagon exercise has highlighted the strategic importance of securing reliable sources of high-purity aluminium while gradually rebuilding domestic manufacturing capability to support long-term defence requirements.

Methodology

How the tables are built

Each Monday AIxEnergy compiles nine standardized tables on electricity demand from data centers and AI from its project database: grid-operator and utility large-load queues, company and regulatory filings, local policy and pushback records, nuclear and geothermal supply deals, and wholesale market prices.
Figures are labeled Observed (counted or summed from source records), Modeled (output of the ELL-2.2.0 large-load realization model) or Analyst estimate. ELL-2.2.0 assigns each queued request a probability of reaching service, calibrated separately for each ISO region to its queue rules, collateral and tariff terms, moratoria and local pushback. Its outputs are estimates, not grid-operator or utility forecasts.
Worksheet 09 maps every column in tables 1 to 8 to its field type (sourced, modeled or derived), database lineage, source ID, source URL and retrieval date. Data rows carry their own source URL and retrieval date. Missing values are left blank.

By table

* Table 1. Active requests in core.large_load_request are counted and summed by operator; realization applies each ISO's ELL-2.2.0 rate.
* Table 2. Campuses are attributed to sponsors; disclosed capital comes from company filings; build-out cost is pipeline GW × an assumed cost per MW.
* Table 3. Rows are verified capital events, one per campus, each with its source URL and retrieval date.

Ohio board approves two gas plants to power adjacent data centres off-grid

Ohio's siting board approved a 1,350 MW gas plant in Fairfield County and an 800 MW one in Pickaway County, each to power a neighbouring data centre off-grid.
From MCR Editor Desk 20 Nov 2026 Fairfield and Pickaway counties, Ohio
The Ohio Power Siting Board (OPSB) on 19 November approved two gas-fired power plants in Ohio, one in Fairfield County and one in Pickaway County. Each will run the data centre beside it and will have no connection to the grid.
The board calls this a "behind-the-meter" set-up: a plant's power serves its neighbouring site rather than the public network. The board's authority covers the generating plants; approving the data centres is outside its remit.
In Fairfield County, Fairfield Energy Center, LLC will build and run a 1,350 MW generating plant and a 1,040 MW battery storage facility on a 122-acre site in the Village of Millersport, Walnut Township, near where State Routes 37 and 204 meet. Fairfield Energy Center says on its own website that the plant will power the Vantage Millersport Campus, a data centre going up next door. Under an agreement with board staff that the OPSB adopted, the company must meet 36 conditions aimed at limiting impacts while the plant is built and operated.
In Pickaway County, PowerConneX, Inc. will build and run the 800 MW Ashville Energy Center on a 110-acre site in the Village of Ashville, on State Route 752 east of State Route 23. The board adopted, with changes, an agreement among PowerConneX, the village and board staff that sets 41 conditions of the same kind, and it requires PowerConneX to keep its financial pledges to the Ashville community. The board's case numbers are 26-160-EL-BGN for Fairfield and 26-196-EL-BGN for Ashville.

About Ohio Power Siting Board and Fairfield Energy Center, LLC

The Ohio Power Siting Board is the state body that must grant a certificate before any major utility facility, including an electric generating plant of 50 MW or more, can be built in Ohio. Created in 1972 as the Ohio Power Siting Commission, it has 11 members: seven voting members, chaired by the head of the Public Utilities Commission, and four non-voting state legislators. It describes its mission as backing energy policies that add generating capacity and transmission for Ohioans while safeguarding land use and the environment.
Fairfield Energy Center is a planned gas-turbine and battery plant of up to 1,350 MW in Millersport, Ohio, built to supply the Vantage Millersport Campus, a data centre next door. Its developer is Advanced Power, which says it develops, manages and owns power infrastructure and already runs Ohio plants including Carroll County Energy and South Field Energy. The project says its batteries, rated at up to 1,040 MW and 2,080 MWh, are there to smooth fast changes in the data centre's demand.

Executive summary

Data centres are increasingly building their own power ‘behind the meter’ (BTM) rather than waiting years for a grid connection. We answer five questions on what that means:
* What is BTM? Power that a data centre produces, stores and uses on its own site. Most sites use it while they wait for a grid connection, but it can stay useful long after the connection arrives.
* How does it vary by region? BTM is largely a US story for now, driven by long grid queues and plentiful gas. Elsewhere, it is smaller and more often powered by renewables.
* Can it compete with the grid on cost? Not on average, but grid constraints, cheap local energy and good financing terms can close much of the gap.
* What else can BTM offer data centres? It can absorb the sudden power swings created by artificial intelligence (AI), cover daily peaks and provide backup, roles that do not end when the grid arrives.
* What does it mean for investors? BTM is more likely to complement the grid than replace it. For grid investors, the bigger risk is speculative demand, although grid operators and regulators are introducing rules to screen it out. We see battery storage as particularly attractive in the value chain, as it remains useful before and after the grid arrives.
BTM may get ahead of the grid, but its long-term value lies alongside it.

What is ‘behind the meter’?

‘Behind the meter’ refers to power generated and stored on the customer’s side of the meter, the point that separates the customer’s own system from the utility’s grid (Figure 1). A household with rooftop solar panels is a small-scale example. At a far larger scale, data centres are increasingly turning to BTM because they cannot afford to wait for the grid. Grid connection queues for data centres have lengthened considerably, a theme we explored in our recent paper, Grid capex in the age of renewables and AI (July 2026). In the main data centre hubs of both the US and Europe, a large new site can now face years of delay while new lines and substations are built. 1

European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers

By Martin Chomsky (Defence Industry Europe)
EU | November 23, 2026
European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
EU defence ministers have endorsed eight opportunities for military cooperation in a review that urges governments to plan capabilities together before taking national procurement decisions. The 2026 Coordinated Annual Review on Defence (CARD), approved on 17 November, identifies opportunities ranging from missiles and unmanned systems to the infrastructure needed to sustain European operations.
The report finds that agreement on defence priorities has not yet translated into a consistently collaborative approach to purchasing equipment. It recommends considering cooperation at the capability planning stage and incorporating it into national programmes and budgets, with projects prepared to draw on EU funding.
Ministers endorsed opportunities to cooperate on a family of cruise missiles, long-range artillery using multiple launch rocket systems and a family of long-range air defence interceptors. They also backed opportunities involving modular, interoperable unmanned ground vehicles and layered counter-drone systems for force protection and critical infrastructure.
The other three opportunities concern space-based early warning, detection and tracking, a European secure defence cloud and a European approach to strategic air mobility. The European Defence Agency (EDA) identifies these as strategic enablers that allow Europe to decide, act and sustain operations autonomously.
“With CARD, we have identified three collaborative opportunities related to strategic enablers,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk. “From space-based early warning to strategic air mobility, and a secure, federated defence cloud architecture, these strategic enablers are essential to strengthening Europe’s deterrence and defence capabilities.”
Their scale, cost and dependence on shared architectures and networks make cooperation necessary, the report says. It argues that no single country can develop and support them alone, while access cannot be assumed in every future contingency.
CARD calls for further analysis, stronger member-state involvement and dedicated roadmaps for these capabilities. That work should build on EDA’s activities and Priority Capability Areas, in coherence with NATO.
The report makes five recommendations covering earlier cooperation, planning beyond 2030, joint work on strategic enablers, the full process of capability development and faster adoption of innovation. It stresses that buying equipment is only part of delivering forces that can deploy and operate effectively.
Personnel, training, doctrine, logistics, sustainment and interoperability increasingly determine how much defence investment becomes usable capability. Shared training capacity, common information-sharing architectures and integration of sensors with command and control offer opportunities that can be delivered faster than large programmes.
The review also identifies delays between promising technological results and operational use. It attributes those delays to experimentation, requirements and acquisition being managed too sequentially and calls for innovation to reach the field faster.
Immediate readiness requirements must be balanced with investment in medium- and long-term needs beyond 2030. The report warns that underinvestment may become visible only after several planning cycles, when correcting it would take considerable time and money.
More systematic cooperation would give manufacturers clearer and more predictable demand, supporting production at scale and reducing supply-chain dependencies. Delivering that cooperation also requires stronger intergovernmental support for joint acquisition, capability development and research.
EDA’s strengthening process is intended to provide that support and help CARD and Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) deliver results. EU incentives, including the European Defence Industry Programme, would support those efforts.
At the 17 November EDA Steering Board, ministers also endorsed a joint statement on defence security of supply. They agreed to increase the agency’s budget.
EDA prepared the report in coordination with the European External Action Service and the EU Military Staff. It is the final deliverable of the fourth CARD cycle, covering 2025–2026.

SECURITY - DEFENCE / Defence

European ministers approve eight opportunities for cooperation

Brussels, 17/11/2026 (Agence Europe)
At a Steering Board of the European Defence Agency (EDA) meeting on Tuesday 17 November, European defence ministers approved eight opportunities for cooperation identified in the ‘ CARD 2026 ’ report.
These include cruise missiles, long-range artillery (multiple-launch rocket systems), modular and interoperable unmanned ground vehicles, layered counter-drone systems to protect critical infrastructure and forces, and families of long-range air-defence interceptors. Three strategic enablers were also approved: space-based early warning, detection, and tracking; the secure European defence ' cloud '; and a European approach to strategic air mobility.
The ‘ CARD 2026 ’ report, which was also approved, sets out five recommendations. According to the report, cooperation should be considered as early as possible. While Member States increasingly agree on priorities, “ cooperation continues to be pursued on an ad hoc basis after national decisions are taken ”, the EDA regrets, calling for cooperation to be built into national programmes and budgets, and for projects eligible for EU funding to be prepared.
The report also calls for planning beyond 2030, which is the date set for defence readiness. Thus, the focus on immediate operational readiness must be accompanied by sustained attention to medium- and long-term needs.
The report also emphasises collaboration on strategic enablers. “ Given their scale, cost and reliance on shared architectures and networks, cooperation here is a necessity, not merely a choice ”, the Agency points out.
The EDA also calls for all aspects of capability development, including personnel, training, doctrine, logistics, support, and interoperability, to be taken into account.
Finally, the report argues for the deployment of innovations in the field to be sped up. It considers that the overly sequential management of experimentation, requirements definition, and procurement mean that promising results too often take too long to become operational capabilities.
See the report: aeur.eu/f/oft
Strengthening security of supply. The ministers also approved a joint declaration on security of supply in defence, stressing that concerted action is needed to reduce undesirable dependencies.
The declaration highlights the need to systematically take defence requirements into consideration in relevant EU initiatives and, where supply is constrained, to ensure that essential defence needs are properly protected and supported.
The ministers also believe that industry needs to take more responsibility for the resilience of its supply chains, and strengthen security of supply. “ EDTIB-based entities and their suppliers should assess and mitigate their exposure to supply chain risks, including through supplier diversification, appropriate redundancy, strategic stockpiling where necessary, and investment in substitutes where technically and economically viable ”, the declaration states.
Finally, the ministers call for more predictable and visible public and private investment, so that industry can sustain the investment needed to increase production capacity.
“ Security of supply [and secure access to critical raw materials] are prerequisites for Defence Readiness 2030 ”, the declaration recalls, stressing that “ EU remains dependent on non-European suppliers for many critical raw materials, chemicals, and components, the availability of which is increasingly determining the pace of capability delivery ”.
Finally, the ministers consider that the Union’s financial and legislative framework, including the future Multiannual Financial Framework, must reflect this urgent need to strengthen security of supply in defence.
See the declaration: aeur.eu/f/ofs
The ministers at their Council meeting also discussed EU-China relations on security and defence, particularly supply issues.

Analysis

Europe Wants China-Free Military Drones. Building the Supply Chain Is the Hard Part.

Europe wants military drones free from vulnerable foreign supply chains, but its manufacturers face a more complicated reality. From critical components and China-free sourcing claims to EU procurement rules.
Daniel Opoku

Daniel Opoku

19 Nov 2026 — 11 min read
Share
Europe Wants China-Free Military Drones. Building the Supply Chain Is the Hard Part. MRM2-10AI at Eurosatory. Photo credit: Orqa FPV
European drone manufacturers face growing pressure to prove where their components originate. But eliminating dependence on Chinese supply chains requires more than transparent sourcing and stricter procurement rules.

...

The difference between European-made and China-free

The origin of a finished drone tells only part of its industrial story.
A flight controller manufactured in Europe may incorporate microcontrollers designed by a European semiconductor company but fabricated, packaged, or tested in different countries. A motor assembled by a European supplier can contain permanent magnets whose raw materials were processed in China. Battery packs may be assembled locally using imported cells, while electronic modules can pass through several countries before reaching a drone manufacturer.
These arrangements are normal features of modern industrial production. They do not automatically indicate poor manufacturing practices, security vulnerabilities, or noncompliance with procurement requirements. They do, however, complicate efforts to establish precisely how independent a product is from a particular country's industrial base.
The distinction becomes especially relevant when manufacturers describe their products as China-free.
That description can be understood in several ways. It might refer to the absence of components manufactured by Chinese companies, components physically produced in China, or particular categories of restricted technology. A more demanding definition might also consider upstream manufacturing processes and the origin of critical raw materials.
These are not necessarily equivalent standards.
A product can be assembled entirely outside China while incorporating materials processed there. Conversely, a component manufactured in China by a Western-owned company may be treated differently under certain procurement regimes than a component designed and manufactured by a Chinese supplier.
Even conventional customs rules do not provide a complete answer.

...

Its experience nonetheless raises a question relevant to manufacturers throughout Europe: how much supply-chain independence can a drone company realistically achieve on its own, and where must national governments and European institutions become part of the solution?

Europe's procurement targets do not tell the whole story

The European Union has already begun introducing requirements intended to encourage domestic defense manufacturing.
The Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument provides up to €150 billion in loans to support defense investment by member states. Under its relevant procurement provisions, components originating outside the EU, the European Economic Area's EFTA states, and Ukraine generally must not exceed 35% of the estimated cost of the end product's components.
The European Defence Industry Programme (EDIP) also includes origin requirements for eligible activities supported through its €1.5 billion grant framework.
These provisions are important steps toward strengthening European defense manufacturing. However, their precise territorial eligibility and other conditions vary by instrument, and the 65% threshold is not a universal rule covering every European military drone.
Neither should it be confused with a guarantee that a product contains no Chinese components.
A percentage-based origin requirement measures a particular form of industrial participation. It does not necessarily establish whether a strategically essential component can be replaced if its supplier becomes unavailable.
A relatively inexpensive electronic component could represent a small proportion of a drone's total component cost while remaining indispensable to its operation.

...

The EU has started financing the answer

The European Commission and Parliament have recognized the need to strengthen the industrial capabilities behind drone production.
In a resolution adopted on January 22, 2026, the European Parliament called for a critical drone component manufacturing action plan, including targeted subsidies for electric motors, lithium batteries, sensors, and additive manufacturing.
Parliament also supported the development of a European drone sovereignty index to assess dependence on suppliers outside the EU and encourage more resilient supply chains.
These recommendations are not equivalent to binding legislation or fully implemented programs, but they indicate growing recognition that European autonomy requires investment beyond complete drone platforms.

...

That does not mean publishing commercially sensitive component inventories or revealing confidential supplier relationships.
A practical verification system could distinguish between final assembly, subsystem manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication and packaging, and the origin of strategically important materials.

Arabian Drilling Secures SAR 1.5 Billion Contract to Run Two KJO Vessels

Arabian Drilling, Saudi Arabia.

By The Edge Research Team
The Takeaway: Arabian Drilling’s SAR 1.5 billion Khafji contract is expected to add to its results from each vessel’s start date, the company said. Its release of 8 November, before the signing, reported record contracted work still to come of SAR 17.6 billion, and the filing does not say how the contract changes that figure. The filing gives no split of value between the vessels and no profit estimate.

Khafji Joint Operations (KJO) has contracted Arabian Drilling to provide and operate two self-propelled offshore service vessels in a SAR 1.5 billion deal, replacing existing contracted service for two vessels.
Arabian Drilling (2381) disclosed the contract to the Saudi Exchange on 22 November. It was published at 05:03 GMT. The filing dates both the award and the signing 19 November, three days earlier, and lists no related parties.

Two vessels, two terms

The contract covers the provision and operation of the two vessels for KJO. They are self-propelled, meaning they move under their own power, and the filing does not say what work they will do. The first is contracted for 10 years and the second for 15. The company expects the first to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028, and it expects the contract to contribute to its results from each start date.
Contract terms by vessel, as disclosed
* Vessel | Term | Expected start
* First | 10 years | Q4 2026
* Second | 15 years | Q4 2028
The filing gives the total value, SAR 1.5 billion, and no value for each vessel.
The filing does not say whether each term runs from the vessel’s start date, from signing or from another date, so end dates cannot be set from it.
Spread evenly over the 25 vessel-years in the two terms, the contract averages SAR 60 million per vessel-year.
That is $16 million at the riyal’s peg of 3.75 to the dollar. The Edge calculated these averages from the filed total. The filing prints no value for each vessel, and unequal rates would change them.
At equal rates, the two vessels would together average SAR 120 million a year once both are running, which the filing expects from the fourth quarter of 2028. The first vessel alone would average SAR 60 million. The release does not say which segment would report the vessels, and they replace existing contracted service, so the value is not all new revenue.

The contract replaces existing vessel service, and the filing’s two texts differ

The English text says the new contract “replaces two existing offshore service vessel contracts”. The Arabic text reads «يحل محل عقد منصتي خدمات بحرية قائمتين», which is one contract covering two existing platforms, and it uses «منصتي» for the new vessels too. The exchange page gives both texts the same date and time, so it does not show which came first.
The Arabic financial-impact line says the contract is expected to contribute to strengthening («تعزيز») the company’s results. Neither text names the counterparty of what is replaced, or gives its value or remaining terms. The filing therefore does not show how much of the contract is additional to what the vessels already earn.

The backlog the company has printed since September

...

It credits two gas awards on land and what it calls the KJO Dorra award covering four offshore rigs. The company’s filings do not use the name Dorra. The match with the 29 September award, on customer and rig count, is The Edge’s reading.
Arabian Drilling contract awards disclosed since 31 August 2026
* Disclosed | Scope | Term | Value as filed
* 31 Aug | SLB, 11 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 3 billion
* 14 Sep | SLB, 8 land rigs, gas | 5 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 29 Sep | KJO, 4 jack-up rigs | 4 years | About SAR 2 billion
* 22 Nov | KJO, 2 service vessels | 10 and 15 years | SAR 1.5 billion
Jack-up rigs are offshore drilling rigs that stand on the seabed. Values are the filings’ own; the first three are stated as approximate.
Two of these four are not new equipment. The 11 land rigs are the incumbent units under the company’s previous gas contract with SLB, and the 8 are redeployed from the existing fleet. SLB is one of the company’s major shareholders, according to the related-parties line of both land filings.
The 29 September award differs in kind. The company said it was the largest single offshore drilling contract KJO has given it, and a 200% increase in the drilling rigs it supplies to KJO. The new contract, by contrast, replaces existing contracted vessel service.
Each filing also says when the award should start to contribute. The company expected the 31 August land award to contribute from the third quarter of 2026, and to support continued use of its land drilling fleet. It expected the 14 September land award to contribute from the fourth quarter.

...

What the company says next

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by approximately 8% to 10% on the third quarter, mainly from the start-up of the gas LSTK and KJO Dorra projects it was awarded. LSTK is the label the filings give the SLB gas work.
That range works out to SAR 876 million to SAR 892 million. The release predates the signing of the vessel contract and does not mention it.
It also raised its 2026 capital spending guidance to SAR 750 million to SAR 800 million, to ready rigs for contracted start dates. The earlier guidance was approximately SAR 700 million.

What the filing leaves out

The filing carries no revenue or profit estimate and no day rates. It does not describe the work the vessels do, name the counterparty of what is being replaced, give its value or end dates, or state any backlog figure.
What to watch: The filing expects the first vessel to begin operating in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the second in the fourth quarter of 2028.
Method: the contract’s value, counterparty, terms, start quarters and replacement are from Arabian Drilling’s announcement on the Saudi Exchange on 22 November 2026.
Backlog, results, segment, fleet, guidance and quotation figures are from the company’s nine-month results announcement and earnings release of 8 November 2026 and its announcements of 12 August, 31 August, 14 September and 29 September.
The per-vessel-year averages, the dollar equivalent at the riyal’s peg of SAR 3.75, the per-unit-year values and the fourth-quarter revenue range are The Edge’s calculations.
Sources: Saudi Exchange, Arabian Drilling, The Edge.

Arabian Drilling Company has signed a long-term contract with Khafji Joint Operations worth 1.5 billion Saudi riyals ($400 million) to provide and operate two self-propelled offshore vessels. The company disclosed the agreement to the Saudi stock exchange, Tadawul, and said it replaces two existing offshore service vessel contracts.

Why it matters

The contract raises Arabian Drilling's backlog to a record of about SAR 18.5 billion, giving the company a longer revenue runway from offshore oil and gas service work. Khafji Joint Operations, a venture between Kuwait Gulf Oil Company and Aramco Gulf Operations Company, is active in onshore and offshore exploration, drilling and production in the Divided Zone.
The 1.5 billion riyal ($400 million) contract covers two offshore vessels, with the first on a 10-year term and the second on a 15-year term. The company has not disclosed annual revenue or margin figures tied to the deal.

The players

Arabian Drilling Company
A Saudi Arabian drilling contractor that provides offshore and onshore drilling and service vessel work to oil and gas operators in the Gulf region.
Khafji Joint Operations
A joint venture between Kuwait Gulf Oil Company and Aramco Gulf Operations Company that conducts oil and gas exploration and production in the Divided Zone.
Tadawul
The Saudi Arabian stock exchange, where listed companies such as Arabian Drilling disclose material agreements to investors.

The details

Under the agreement, Arabian Drilling will provide and operate two self-propelled offshore vessels for Khafji Joint Operations, replacing two existing offshore service vessel contracts. The contract will contribute to the company's financial results as each vessel becomes operational.

Timeline

1. Fourth quarter of 2026: the first vessel begins its 10-year contract operations.
2. Fourth quarter of 2028: the second vessel begins its 15-year contract operations.

The deal extends the Divided Zone partnership between Kuwait Gulf Oil Company and Aramco Gulf Operations Company by adding offshore vessel capacity to the existing joint operations. For individual investors, the contract is disclosed to Tadawul and adds multi-year revenue visibility, though its earnings effect depends on when each vessel becomes operational. The deal does not directly change fuel prices or product availability for consumers.

The takeaway

A large multi-year contract can lift a service company's backlog substantially, but investors should watch when each asset starts generating revenue rather than the headline contract value alone.

Arabian Drilling won a SAR 1.5 billion contract from Khafji Joint Operations for two self-propelled service platforms.
Key Points
1. Arabian Drilling won a SAR 1.5 billion contract from Khafji Joint Operations for two self-propelled service platforms.
2. Terms run 10 years for the first platform and 15 years for the second.
3. The deal replaces an existing two-platform contract, locking in Khafji revenue into the 2040s.
The latest:
Arabian Drilling has signed a SAR 1.5 billion long-term contract with Khafji Joint Operations to supply and operate two self-propelled offshore service platforms, according to the company’s disclosure to the Saudi Exchange. The agreement replaces an existing contract covering two platforms already in service. The first unit carries a 10-year term, the second 15 years.
Details:
* The value: The company put the contract at SAR 1.5 billion, covering the provision and operation of two self-propelled offshore service platforms for Khafji Joint Operations. The disclosure did not break the figure down between the two units or specify day rates.
* The counterparty: Khafji Joint Operations is the contracting entity. Arabian Drilling stated there are no related parties involved in the agreement, meaning the award falls outside related-party transaction disclosure requirements.
* The terms: The first platform is contracted for 10 years, the second for 15 years. Both terms run from each unit’s own start of operations rather than from signing, extending Arabian Drilling’s revenue visibility at Khafji well beyond the current decade.
* Replacement, not addition: The company said the new agreement replaces an existing contract for two offshore service platforms already working for Khafji. That framing matters for modelling: part of the SAR 1.5 billion substitutes for revenue the company was already booking rather than adding entirely new work.
* The dates: Arabian Drilling said the award was announced and the contract signed on 19 November 2026, corresponding to 9 Jumada al-Akhirah 1448. The disclosure was filed with the Saudi Exchange on 22 November 2026 at 08:03.
* Financial impact: The company expects the contract to strengthen its financial results from the start of operations of each platform — the fourth quarter of 2026 for the first unit and the fourth quarter of 2028 for the second. No earnings estimate was attached to either phase.
* The two-year gap: The staggered start dates mean roughly two years separate the two revenue streams, with the second platform’s contribution not landing until late 2028. Arabian Drilling did not disclose whether capital spending is required ahead of that second start-up.
* The share reaction: Arabian Drilling, listed under code 2381 on the Saudi Exchange, was quoted down 2.40% alongside the disclosure.
Background:
Khafji Joint Operations runs production in the Partitioned Neutral Zone shared by Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. Offshore service platforms there support drilling, workover and maintenance activity, and are typically contracted on multi-year terms that tie a contractor’s fleet to a single field for the full duration.
Between the lines:
The structure of the award is as notable as its size. Because the contract supersedes an existing two-platform deal rather than sitting alongside it, the headline SAR 1.5 billion overstates the incremental revenue. What the company gains is duration: terms of 10 and 15 years convert work already in hand into contracted backlog stretching toward 2041 for the second unit, a form of visibility the market usually values more than a single year’s uplift.
What’s next
The first platform’s start-up in the fourth quarter of 2026 is the near-term marker, with any contribution showing in the company’s Q4 results. The second unit’s late-2028 start is the next scheduled trigger.

Saipem has secured two offshore drilling contracts worth approximately $181m for its Scarabeo 9 semi-submersible in Egypt and Suriname, with work due to start in 2027.
TotalEnergies EP Suriname has awarded the rig a campaign covering five wells offshore Suriname, with an option for five more.
That work is scheduled to follow an assignment in Egypt, where Burullus Gas has contracted Scarabeo 9 to drill three offshore wells.
Operations in Egypt are due to begin in the first quarter of 2027. Burullus is a joint venture between Shell, Petronas and the state-owned Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation (EGPC).
Saipem said the contracts add to its offshore drilling fleet backlog and provide greater visibility over Scarabeo 9 's utilisation through 2027 and 2028. It also said the awards strengthen its long-standing relationships with Burullus and TotalEnergies.
Scarabeo 9 is an ultra-deepwater drilling unit equipped with a dual RamRig and a DP3 dynamic positioning system.
It is designed to operate in water depths of up to 12,000ft and drill to 50,000ft below the rotary table. Its permanent accommodation module has a capacity for 200 people.
In a separate development earlier, ExxonMobil Guyana authorised Saipem to proceed with the Longtail project in the Stabroek Block offshore Guyana. The project is located in water depths of around 1,750m.
Saipem had received a limited notice to proceed on 21 April 2026 for preliminary detailed engineering and the procurement of long-lead equipment.
